1:
What is technology? We use this word regularly, but how should we define it? And what does this definition give us?

The word comes from ancient Greek: tékhnê, which refers to manual skill, craft, know-how; and logos, which refers to speech, discourse, knowledge. Technology is therefore the meeting of the two: doing and knowing.

More formally, we can say that technology is a set of means used to achieve a goal. It involves three things: knowledge, particularly scientific knowledge; procedures, that is, ways of doing things; and artefacts, concrete objects.

An important distinction: technology is not technique. Technique is empirical know-how, a knack, like that of a luthier making a violin or of a top athlete. It cannot be codified in a manual. Technology, on the other hand, combines this know-how with knowledge – in particular scientific knowledge – which can be passed on, learned and written down.

And this is where it becomes interesting for management: what matters is not only the object, it is the knowledge behind it. The companies that dominate artificial intelligence today did not develop the best tools by chance; they managed to attract the people who hold the knowledge and know-how needed to implement these tools.

This last point shows the essential role that skills management plays in the management of technology.
2:
An essential definition for this course: what is innovation?

Innovation is often confused with invention. They are not the same thing. Invention is the good idea, the “eureka!” moment. There are also perfectly useless, even far-fetched inventions that will never really be adopted: interesting ideas that find no use.

Innovation is something else: it is the realisation of novelty.

This word, “realisation”, is central. An invention becomes an innovation when it moves into action, when it is implemented, when it finds its market, when it becomes part of everyday habits.

More analytically, innovation can be defined as the process of putting something new into practice in order to create value.

Managing innovation means managing this process.

And this goes far beyond the question of creativity, because having a good idea is only a very small part of the journey, the first steps. The longest and most difficult part is all the work that remains to turn the good idea into something that works, that finds its market, that creates value. It is precisely this work that this course will teach you to manage.

Another useful point: the word innovation refers both to a process and to an outcome. When I say that a product is an innovation, I am talking about the outcome. When I ask how a company managed to create this product, I am talking about the process. In this course, we will talk about both, but the main question will be the process: how to develop a company’s ability to implement new things that create value.
3:
A characteristic of innovation to keep in mind: innovation is a major economic and strategic issue.

A few elements support this idea. Theoretical ones first.

Joseph Schumpeter, the father of the economics of innovation, put forward this idea very early on: innovation is, in his view, the essential source of competition, economic development and the transformation of society. More recently, Philippe Aghion received the 2025 Nobel Prize in Economics for extending Schumpeter’s work on what is called creative destruction: the idea that technological innovations constantly replace established technologies and existing companies. Apple and its iPhone replacing Nokia and its mobile phones – thereby taking its place as industry leader – that is this very dynamic. The great theorists of strategic management (for example Michael Porter, Jay Barney, David Teece) have also taken this reality into account in their work.

This is not just a theoretical intuition. The World Economic Forum builds a global competitiveness index of economies, and innovation capacity is among the most decisive criteria, once the fundamentals are in place. And if we cross international innovation rankings with economic competitiveness rankings, such as the IMD’s, we find the same countries at the top: in the European Union, Denmark, Sweden and Finland. The link between a country’s innovation capacity and its competitiveness is strong.

So remember this: innovation is not a secondary or incidental subject. It is one of the most powerful drivers of the economy and of corporate strategy, and that is precisely why we are devoting an entire management course to it.
4:
Another characteristic of innovation, and an important one to understand properly: innovation is not solely a technological matter.

Take the example of Apple. When we think of the iPhone or the iPod, we immediately think of a technological feat. But is that really Apple’s innovation? Not only. There is design, of course, which is not a scientific matter in itself. There is marketing, the way Apple has staged its products, notably at its famous autumn keynotes. And above all, there is the business model: with the App Store and iTunes, Apple does not merely sell a device; the company also controls the entire distribution channel for the apps and music that go through that device. That is where innovation plays out, as much as in the technology itself.

Even in a sector we might think of as purely technological, such as solar panels, there is much more at stake than the performance of photovoltaic cells. There are environmental factors, the fight against global warming. Political factors: not all governments care about it to the same degree. Social factors: acceptability, a bit like wind turbines, which are sometimes criticised on aesthetic grounds. Economic factors, such as the price at which an electricity supplier buys back the surplus produced. And even geopolitical factors, linked to access to the mineral resources needed for manufacturing, or to the price of hydrocarbons, which are an alternative to electricity.

So remember this: even when an innovation has a strong technological dimension, having the best technology is never enough. You need to understand the whole environment – market, society, politics – to make it succeed.
5:
There are different types of innovation.

A first essential distinction: technological innovation and market innovation. Market innovation consists in offering something new (a new product or a new market); technological innovation consists in using a new technology.

The transistor is a purely technological innovation, the basis of all modern electronics. Airbnb, by contrast, is a market innovation: it is a matchmaking platform that does not rely on any particular technical feat, just a good idea well executed. And the two are often combined: the transistor radio of the 1950s was both a technological innovation, through the use of the transistor, and a market innovation, because it made possible and accessible a new product: the portable radio.

A second distinction: the degree of innovation. We speak of radical innovation when something completely new appears, such as the very first iPhone. And of incremental innovation when the existing is gradually improved, such as the later versions of the same iPhone. This boundary is never entirely clear-cut: it is often a matter of perception and degree, and even the innovations that seem most radical to us always build, in reality, on what existed before.

Finally, innovations can be classified according to their nature. Product innovation is a new or improved good, such as a foldable smartphone. Service innovation concerns an intangible offer: this is the case of Uber, which offers a service connecting drivers and passengers. Process innovation concerns the way things are made or delivered, like the standardised production line that allowed McDonald’s to serve its customers faster. And business model innovation concerns the way money is made: this is what Netflix did when it moved from renting DVDs by mail to streaming subscriptions.

Remember this analytical grid: technological or market, radical or incremental, and product, service, process or business model. It will serve us throughout the course to analyse concrete cases of innovation.
